papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods form a diverse toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Approaches include classic soft-label distillation, intermediate-representation (layer/hint) matching, contrastive and distributional alignment, adversarial and robustness-focused strategies, teacher-design and selection methods, and structural compression (e.g., pruning and progressive module replacement). Empirical work across vision, NLP, ranking, translation, summarization, reinforcement learning, and 3D/pose tasks demonstrates practical trade-offs between accuracy, robustness, data requirements, and inference latency.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students). Approaches span soft-target (logit) matching, transferring intermediate/internal representations, layer-wise and module-level mimicry, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision and NLP shows KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance, but success depends on factors such as teacher-student capacity gap, the form of distilled knowledge, task alignment, and the data used for distillation. Contemporary research emphasizes task-aware selection of distilled signals, improving teacher-student compatibility, and preserving robustness and decision-boundary information to make distillation more effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to deploy large deep models by training smaller students to capture the behavior of larger teachers or ensembles. Work across computer vision, NLP, and reinforcement learning has developed complementary approaches: soft-target distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, multi- and online-teacher strategies, confidence- and task-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and techniques that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. These methods trade off fidelity to the teacher, training cost, data requirements, robustness, and runtime efficiency; their empirical success depends on design choices such as what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations), how teachers are selected or learned, and whether the process is offline, online, or self-distillation. The literature shows that (1) distillation often reduces the effective complexity of training data and eases learning for constrained student architectures, (2) internal-representation losses, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, and route or curriculum strategies can substantially improve transfer, and (3) distillation can be combined with pruning or adversarial objectives to yield compact, fast, and sometimes robust models. Practical application requires matching the distillation recipe to task characteristics, data availability, and the student capacity.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods form a diverse and practically effective toolbox for producing smaller, faster models from large neural networks. Practitioners combine techniques that transfer output distributions, align internal representations, replace modules progressively, or apply structured pruning; adaptions such as multi-teacher schedules, meta-learned teachers, task-aware filters, and adversarial objectives address capacity gaps, data complexity, and robustness. Careful matching of distillation recipe, student capacity, and task constraints yields the best trade-offs between latency, memory, and retained performance.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones in both vision and NLP. KD works through multiple mechanisms — smoothing, class-relationship transfer, and instance-level guidance — and can be combined with complementary techniques such as structured pruning, module replacement, and curriculum-style training. Practical success depends on aligning the distilled signals with the student capacity and the target task: task-aware selection of teacher information, attention to internal representations, dynamic or meta-learned teacher strategies, and robustness-aware objectives all improve outcomes. Depending on constraints (data availability, latency, robustness), alternatives like structured pruning or parameter shrinking may be preferable or used in concert with KD.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: A Task-Aware, Representation-Centric Case for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When designed to transfer the right form of knowledge for the target task and student capacity — e.g., soft targets, intermediate representations, decision-boundary signals, or teacher trajectories — distillation can deliver strong trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy. Best results arise when distillation is combined with task-aware selection of teacher signals, teacher scheduling or meta-weighting, and complementary compression such as structured pruning. I argue that representation- and task-aware distillation, augmented by robustness- and capacity-aware teacher design, offers the most reliable path for model compression in real-world NLP and deep learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation as the Most Reliable Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones. Empirical and theoretical work indicates KD succeeds most consistently when it transfers the internal, task-relevant representations that matter for the downstream objective, mitigates teacher–student capability gaps via adaptive teacher strategies, and is combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when latency or data constraints demand it. I argue that a practical, high-performing distillation pipeline should therefore (1) be task-aware in selecting which representations to transfer, (2) align intermediate features rather than only soft logits when student capacity permits, (3) use adaptive or multi-teacher schedules to close capability gaps, and (4) integrate complementary methods like progressive replacement and pruning when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, flexible approach for producing compact models from large teachers. When distillation explicitly targets internal representations and is adapted to task constraints, teacher–student capacity gaps, and robustness requirements, it yields the best practical tradeoffs for accuracy, latency, and model footprint in both vision and NLP. However, KD is not universally optimal: simple parameter shrinking or pseudo-labeling can outperform complex distillation in some settings, and careful choice or combination of distillation recipes (soft targets, representation matching, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- or evolving teachers, and pruning hybrids) is required to meet particular deployment constraints. I argue that adopting task-aware, representation-focused KD—combined selectively with pruning or progressive module replacement and with attention to teacher design and robustness—provides the most reliable path to high-quality compressed models in practice.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and its Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning based models are relatively large, and it is hard to deploy such models on resource-limited devices such as mobile phones and embedded devices. One possible solution is knowledge distillation whereby a smaller model (student model) is trained by utilizing the information from a larger model (teacher model). In this paper, we present a survey of knowledge distillation techniques applied to deep learning models. To compare the performances of different techniques, we propose a new metric called distillation metric. Distillation metric compares different knowledge distillation algorithms based on sizes and accuracy scores. Based on the survey, some interesting conclusions are drawn and presented in this paper.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer the predictive power of large models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Research across vision, reinforcement learning, and NLP has produced a wide set of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate representation matching, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum-based routes, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structured pruning—that trade off fidelity, compute cost, and data requirements. Empirical results show KD can recover much of teacher performance in many settings, but success depends on teacher-student capacity gaps, the form of transferred knowledge, availability of data, and task properties. The literature has proposed principled analyses and practical recipes for improving transfer, consolidating state-of-the-art compression workflows for NLP tasks such as classification, translation, ranking, and summarization.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, empirically effective core strategy for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. When applied as a task-aware, representation-focused toolkit and combined with adaptive teacher selection, curriculum-like schedules, or complementary compression (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation reliably yields high-quality students while addressing practical constraints such as latency, memory, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a model-agnostic technique to improve model quality while having a fixed capacity budget. It is a commonly used technique for model compression, where a larger capacity teacher model with better quality is used to train a more compact student model with better inference efficiency. Through distillation, one hopes to benefit from student's compactness, without sacrificing too much on model quality. Despite the large success of knowledge distillation, better understanding of how it benefits student model's training dynamics remains under-explored. In this paper, we categorize teacher's knowledge into three hierarchical levels and study its effects on knowledge distillation: (1) knowledge of the `universe', where KD brings a regularization effect through label smoothing; (2) domain knowledge, where teacher injects class relationships prior to student's logit layer geometry; and (3) instance specific knowledge, where teacher rescales student model's per-instance gradients based on its measurement on the event difficulty. Using systematic analyses and extensive empirical studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we confirm that the aforementioned three factors play a major role in knowledge distillation. Furthermore, based on our findings, we diagnose some of the failure cases of applying KD from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes the main mechanisms, strategies, empirical findings, and practical trade-offs for knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It outlines what of the teacher to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention and inter-channel structure), how to adapt distillation to task and student capacity (task-aware layer selection, adaptive teacher weighting, self-distillation, and meta-teaching), and when to combine KD with complementary compression methods (structured pruning, progressive module replacement, and adversarially-aware training). The synthesis highlights recurring practical constraints—teacher–student capacity gap, data requirements, robustness concerns, and latency vs accuracy trade-offs—and sketches commonly recommended strategies to address them.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques create smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. The field has developed a broad set of complementary strategies — soft-label (logit) distillation, internal/feature-level matching, attention- and correlation-based objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, self-distillation and meta-learned teachers, adversarial and curriculum-based methods, and hybrids that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. Practical effectiveness depends on matching what is transferred and how it is scheduled to the task, the teacher–student capacity gap, and data availability; hybrid approaches that attend to task-relevant representations and robustness tend to offer the best operational trade-offs for NLP deployments.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. A wide range of KD strategies—matching soft targets, aligning internal representations, adversarial transfers, multi-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement—have proven effective across vision, ranking, and NLP tasks. Best results arise when distillation methods are chosen or combined to match the task and constraints: internal- and layer-wise alignment help transfer structural features, teacher training and trajectory-aware approaches improve transferability, adversarial and contrastive formulations capture richer knowledge, and alternatives such as structured pruning or simplified shrink-and-fine-tune procedures can be preferable under specific data or latency constraints. Practical adoption therefore benefits from a taxonomy of KD techniques and task-aware selection of methods.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of approaches for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance of large teacher models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned student-friendly teachers, evolutionary or online teachers, multi-teacher ensembles), and whether complementary compression such as pruning is used. Empirical work across vision, NLP, ranking, summarization and reinforcement learning shows that targeted choices about the distillation signal, teacher selection, and task-awareness substantially affect student quality, robustness, and inference efficiency. Remaining challenges include closing capability gaps between teachers and students, reducing dependence on large unlabeled datasets, and ensuring transfer of internal and robustness properties.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods form a broad, practical toolbox for producing compact, faster models from large deep networks. Research has extended simple soft-target matching to many complementary strategies — internal representation alignment, attention- and feature-based matching, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, and integration with structured pruning. Empirical work across NLP subfields (classification, ranking, summarization, translation, and detection) shows that method choice should be driven by student capacity, task complexity, data availability, and desired trade-offs between latency, accuracy, and robustness. A consistent theme is that selectively transferring the representations and signals most relevant to the target task, and adapting the distillation schedule to reduce teacher–student gaps, yields the most reliable practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring information from large teacher models into compact students. The literature shows a broad set of mechanisms (soft-target transfer, internal-representation alignment, contrastive/adversarial objectives, and progressive module replacement), multiple teacher–student design patterns (fixed, evolving, multi-teacher, and student-friendly teachers), and practical hybrids with pruning or module-replacement strategies. Empirical work across NLP, vision, translation, summarization, non-autoregressive generation, and structured prediction demonstrates the importance of matching the distillation recipe to task constraints, student capacity, and data availability. Major open issues remain around closing teacher–student capability gaps, reducing dependence on large or carefully distilled datasets for sequence tasks, and ensuring reliable transfer of internal representations and robustness properties.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD’s practical success depends on selecting the right distilled signals (soft labels, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial/contrastive signals), managing teacher–student capacity gaps, and accounting for task-specific constraints such as data availability, latency, and robustness. When combined with adaptive teacher strategies and complementary compression methods (pruning, progressive module replacement), representation- and task-aware distillation yields the best tradeoffs between size, speed, accuracy, and robustness for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation via Route Constrained Optimization
papers_seen.abstract: Distillation-based learning boosts the performance of the miniaturized neural network based on the hypothesis that the representation of a teacher model can be used as structured and relatively weak supervision, and thus would be easily learned by a miniaturized model. However, we find that the representation of a converged heavy model is still a strong constraint for training a small student model, which leads to a high lower bound of congruence loss. In this work, inspired by curriculum learning we consider the knowledge distillation from the perspective of curriculum learning by routing. Instead of supervising the student model with a converged teacher model, we supervised it with some anchor points selected from the route in parameter space that the teacher model passed by, as we called route constrained optimization (RCO). We experimentally demonstrate this simple operation greatly reduces the lower bound of congruence loss for knowledge distillation, hint and mimicking learning. On close-set classification tasks like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, RCO improves knowledge distillation by 2.14% and 1.5% respectively. For the sake of evaluating the generalization, we also test RCO on the open-set face recognition task MegaFace.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while retaining performance. The field has diversified from simple soft-target matching to include intermediate-representation alignment, attention- and feature-based matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with pruning. Practical success depends on matching the form of transferred knowledge to student capacity and task demands, managing data and robustness trade-offs, and often combining KD with complementary compression techniques or task-aware selection of signals. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, training paradigms, practical considerations, representative methods, and open challenges to guide application and research in KD for deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation as the Most Reliable Path to Compact and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. I argue that the most reliable and practical path for high-quality compressed models in NLP is a combined strategy that (1) prioritizes representation-focused, task-aware transfer (selectively aligning intermediate features relevant to the target task), (2) uses adaptive teacher schedules and multi-teacher weighting to manage capability gaps, and (3) integrates distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacement). This hybrid stance balances accuracy, robustness, and computational cost while addressing dataset complexity and student capacity constraints.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Improving Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: This paper explores the use of knowledge distillation to improve a Multi-Task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) (Liu et al., 2019) for learning text representations across multiple natural language understanding tasks. Although ensemble learning can improve model performance, serving an ensemble of large DNNs such as MT-DNN can be prohibitively expensive. Here we apply the knowledge distillation method (Hinton et al., 2015) in the multi-task learning setting. For each task, we train an ensemble of different MT-DNNs (teacher) that outperforms any single model, and then train a single MT-DNN (student) via multi-task learning to \emph{distill} knowledge from these ensemble teachers. We show that the distilled MT-DNN significantly outperforms the original MT-DNN on 7 out of 9 GLUE tasks, pushing the GLUE benchmark (single model) to 83.7\% (1.5\% absolute improvement\footnote{ Based on the GLUE leaderboard at https://gluebenchmark.com/leaderboard as of April 1, 2019.}). The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/namisan/mt-dnn.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible and effective approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment. Across vision, language, and structured prediction tasks, distillation methods that go beyond matching output logits—by leveraging intermediate representations, adaptive teacher-student interaction, adversarial examples, and task-aware selection—consistently improve student performance while addressing practical constraints such as inference speed, memory, and robustness. Combining distillation with complementary techniques (progressive replacing, pruning, or route-constrained supervision) further mitigates capacity gaps and teacher limitations, making distillation a practical centerpiece of model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from teacher models to student models. Research has advanced along multiple axes: (1) what knowledge is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations, decision-boundary samples, etc.), (2) when and how the teacher and student are trained (offline pre-trained teachers, joint / online / evolutionary teachers, meta-learned teachers, progressive replacement), (3) specialized objectives and architectures for transfer (adversarial objectives, Wasserstein-based contrastive losses, layer-wise/task-aware filters, route-constrained curricula), and (4) applications and tradeoffs in domains such as image classification, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, ranking, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Empirical work shows that appropriate choice of knowledge, coupling between teacher and student, and task-aware filtering substantially affects final student accuracy, robustness, and latency. Ongoing challenges include closing the capacity gap for very small students, preserving robustness and internal representations, and reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora for distillation.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer the predictive power of large models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Research across vision, reinforcement learning, and NLP has produced a wide set of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate representation matching, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum-based routes, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structured pruning—that trade off fidelity, compute cost, and data requirements. Empirical results show KD can recover much of teacher performance in many settings, but success depends on teacher-student capacity gaps, the form of transferred knowledge, availability of data, and task properties. The literature has proposed principled analyses and practical recipes for improving transfer, consolidating state-of-the-art compression workflows for NLP tasks such as classification, translation, ranking, and summarization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: The State of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Mechanisms, Challenges, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective class of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. KD works through multiple mechanisms—soft-label transfer, internal-representation matching, contrastive and adversarial objectives, progressive module replacement, and meta- or curriculum-based teacher design—and has been adapted to many domains including NLP, machine translation, summarization, ranking, detection, and reinforcement learning. While KD can deliver large gains in inference speed and storage efficiency with modest drops in performance, its success depends on matching distillation strategy to task and student capacity, addressing teacher-student capability gaps, and attending to robustness and data requirements. Practical compression pipelines benefit from combining distillation with structured pruning, task-aware layer selection, or robustness-aware objectives to maximize latency, accuracy, and stability trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from teacher models to student models. Research has advanced along multiple axes: (1) what knowledge is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations, decision-boundary samples, etc.), (2) when and how the teacher and student are trained (offline pre-trained teachers, joint / online / evolutionary teachers, meta-learned teachers, progressive replacement), (3) specialized objectives and architectures for transfer (adversarial objectives, Wasserstein-based contrastive losses, layer-wise/task-aware filters, route-constrained curricula), and (4) applications and tradeoffs in domains such as image classification, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, ranking, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Empirical work shows that appropriate choice of knowledge, coupling between teacher and student, and task-aware filtering substantially affects final student accuracy, robustness, and latency. Ongoing challenges include closing the capacity gap for very small students, preserving robustness and internal representations, and reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora for distillation.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods form a broad, practical toolbox for producing compact, faster models from large deep networks. Research has extended simple soft-target matching to many complementary strategies — internal representation alignment, attention- and feature-based matching, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, and integration with structured pruning. Empirical work across NLP subfields (classification, ranking, summarization, translation, and detection) shows that method choice should be driven by student capacity, task complexity, data availability, and desired trade-offs between latency, accuracy, and robustness. A consistent theme is that selectively transferring the representations and signals most relevant to the target task, and adapting the distillation schedule to reduce teacher–student gaps, yields the most reliable practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining performance. Across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, reinforcement learning, and many NLP tasks, complementary strategies — matching soft targets, aligning intermediate representations (features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations), adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi- and evolving-teacher schemes, and hybrids with pruning or progressive module replacement — have been shown effective. Practical success depends on matching the distillation recipe to task properties, student capacity, and data or latency constraints; common failure modes trace to large teacher–student gaps, limited distillation data, and overly narrow transfer signals. This synthesis summarizes the mechanisms, practical strategies, empirical findings, and remaining challenges that researchers and practitioners face when using KD for model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and its Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning based models are relatively large, and it is hard to deploy such models on resource-limited devices such as mobile phones and embedded devices. One possible solution is knowledge distillation whereby a smaller model (student model) is trained by utilizing the information from a larger model (teacher model). In this paper, we present a survey of knowledge distillation techniques applied to deep learning models. To compare the performances of different techniques, we propose a new metric called distillation metric. Distillation metric compares different knowledge distillation algorithms based on sizes and accuracy scores. Based on the survey, some interesting conclusions are drawn and presented in this paper.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: A Task-Aware, Representation-Centric Case for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When designed to transfer the right form of knowledge for the target task and student capacity — e.g., soft targets, intermediate representations, decision-boundary signals, or teacher trajectories — distillation can deliver strong trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy. Best results arise when distillation is combined with task-aware selection of teacher signals, teacher scheduling or meta-weighting, and complementary compression such as structured pruning. I argue that representation- and task-aware distillation, augmented by robustness- and capacity-aware teacher design, offers the most reliable path for model compression in real-world NLP and deep learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central to Efficient NLP Models — and How to Make It Better
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Its success spans supervised tasks, multi-task systems, ensembles, and specialized settings like non-autoregressive translation, ranking, and summarization. However, distillation has known weaknesses (data requirements, capacity gaps, robustness) that motivate complementary or improved algorithms. Combining distillation with task-aware, representational, adversarial, or pruning-based techniques produces more compact and reliable models suitable for production NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become core tools for transferring knowledge from larger, expensive models to smaller, efficient models. Research has developed multiple complementary strategies — logit/soft-label distillation, internal/feature-level matching, layer-wise and module-wise transfer, multi-teacher and ensemble-based approaches, adversarial and curriculum-based methods, and combinations with pruning — and applied them across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning tasks. Advances emphasize matching representations that matter for a target task, selecting trustworthy or tightly-coupled supervision signals, and shaping the distillation process (e.g., via progressive replacement, teacher evolution, or task-aware filtering) to close capability gaps between teacher and student while preserving performance, robustness, and runtime efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: A Task-Aware, Representation-Centric Defense of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. The most reliable-distillation workflows prioritize transferring task-relevant internal representations, adaptively selecting and weighting teacher signals, and combining distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., pruning or progressive module replacement) when constraints demand it. Success requires addressing capacity gaps, data limitations, and robustness concerns via task-aware layer selection, confidence-aware teacher weighting, and adversarial or contrastive training signals. When applied with these principles, KD yields substantial gains in latency and footprint while preserving much of the performance of large models across vision, ranking, translation, and other NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: The Case for Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into efficient students for deployment. However, its success is not uniform: different distillation strategies transfer different kinds of knowledge, interact with model capacity and data complexity, and trade off accuracy, robustness, and cost. I argue that the most reliable path to compact, high-quality models—especially in NLP—is to adopt task-aware, representation-focused distillation that (1) aligns intermediate representations selectively to the target task, (2) uses adaptive teacher schedules or multi-teacher weighting to reduce capability gaps, and (3) integrates distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacing). This combined stance balances effectiveness, computational cost, and robustness, and is supported by empirical and theoretical analyses across vision, language, retrieval, and sequence generation settings.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students). Over the past decade methods have moved beyond simple output-probability (soft-label) matching to leverage internal representations, layer-wise alignment, adversarial objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble sources, online or evolving teachers, and task-aware compression strategies. In NLP, KD is widely used to compress large pretrained transformers for downstream tasks, but choices about what to transfer and how to schedule or weight supervision have important trade-offs for accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Key open challenges include closing the teacher–student capacity gap, reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora for distillation, and preserving robustness and task-specific information while obtaining practical speedups.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Exploring Inter-Channel Correlation for Diversity-preserved KnowledgeDistillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation has shown very promising abil-ity in transferring learned representation from the largermodel (teacher) to the smaller one (student).Despitemany efforts, prior methods ignore the important role ofretaining inter-channel correlation of features, leading tothe lack of capturing intrinsic distribution of the featurespace and sufficient diversity properties of features in theteacher network.To solve the issue, we propose thenovel Inter-Channel Correlation for Knowledge Distillation(ICKD), with which the diversity and homology of the fea-ture space of the student network can align with that ofthe teacher network. The correlation between these twochannels is interpreted as diversity if they are irrelevantto each other, otherwise homology. Then the student isrequired to mimic the correlation within its own embed-ding space. In addition, we introduce the grid-level inter-channel correlation, making it capable of dense predictiontasks. Extensive experiments on two vision tasks, includ-ing ImageNet classification and Pascal VOC segmentation,demonstrate the superiority of our ICKD, which consis-tently outperforms many existing methods, advancing thestate-of-the-art in the fields of Knowledge Distillation. Toour knowledge, we are the first method based on knowl-edge distillation boosts ResNet18 beyond 72% Top-1 ac-curacy on ImageNet classification. Code is available at:https://github.com/ADLab-AutoDrive/ICKD.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches range from matching output probabilities to aligning intermediate representations, using single or multiple teachers, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filtering. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows distillation can improve student accuracy, speed, and sometimes robustness, but its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gap, the form of transferred knowledge, data availability, and task-specific constraints. Complementary compression methods such as structured pruning can match or exceed distillation on some latency metrics while avoiding unlabeled-data costs. Recent innovations focus on better aligning internal representations, dynamically selecting or evolving teachers, preserving robustness, and reducing the difficulty gap between teacher and student to improve transfer.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, empirically effective core strategy for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. When applied as a task-aware, representation-focused toolkit and combined with adaptive teacher selection, curriculum-like schedules, or complementary compression (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement), distillation reliably yields high-quality students while addressing practical constraints such as latency, memory, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. A wide range of KD strategies—matching soft targets, aligning internal representations, adversarial transfers, multi-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement—have proven effective across vision, ranking, and NLP tasks. Best results arise when distillation methods are chosen or combined to match the task and constraints: internal- and layer-wise alignment help transfer structural features, teacher training and trajectory-aware approaches improve transferability, adversarial and contrastive formulations capture richer knowledge, and alternatives such as structured pruning or simplified shrink-and-fine-tune procedures can be preferable under specific data or latency constraints. Practical adoption therefore benefits from a taxonomy of KD techniques and task-aware selection of methods.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP (2017–2022)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Across vision, speech, reinforcement learning and NLP, the field has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, feature-map and inter-channel correlation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, module-replacement and progressive shrinking, and hybrid approaches that combine distillation with structured pruning. Empirical work shows these techniques can preserve accuracy while delivering large parameter and latency reductions, but success depends on choices such as what to transfer (logits vs. intermediate features), how to schedule or construct the teacher (fixed, learned, or progressive), the student capacity and task complexity, and available unlabeled data. Recent efforts also address robustness, decision-boundary alignment, and task-aware filtering, and alternative compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning) can match distillation in some settings when combined with task-specific transfer. Remaining challenges include capacity gaps between teachers and students, the need for large or carefully distilled data in sequence-generation tasks, and ensuring reliable transfer of internal structure rather than only matching outputs.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, ranking, detection, and reinforcement learning. The literature converges on three broad ideas: (1) KD works via multiple complementary mechanisms—soft-target transfer, internal-representation alignment, and instance- or curriculum-level guidance—that ease student learning; (2) careful teacher design and the match between teacher signals and student capacity are decisive for success; and (3) KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (structured pruning, module replacement, routing curricula) and with robustness- or task-aware objectives. Important open problems remain, including closing teacher–student capability gaps, reducing reliance on large unlabeled datasets, preserving adversarial robustness, and choosing cost-effective distillation recipes for particular deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy large deep models by transferring aspects of teacher models into smaller students, or by surgically removing capacity via pruning. Research across vision, NLP, ranking, reinforcement learning and 3D detection has developed many complementary distillation formulations (soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, layer-wise alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and pruning-aware strategies) as well as strategies for choosing or evolving teachers. Results show that distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while improving latency and storage, can improve robustness or continual-learning behavior when adapted appropriately, and interacts nontrivially with dataset complexity and student capacity. Practical trade-offs remain: some distillation variants require extra unlabeled data or expensive teacher ensembles, while pruning-based methods can achieve high sparsity and speedups without distillation at the cost of different engineering considerations.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, efficient models by transferring information from one or more teacher models to a student model. The literature shows a wide variety of objectives and mechanisms for KD — from soft-target matching and internal representation alignment to adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-inspired routes — and covers applications across vision, ranking, summarization, machine translation, and reinforcement learning. Trade-offs reported across studies include teacher–student capacity gap effects, data requirements, computational cost, robustness and generalization properties, and task-specific adaptations. Practical recipes include multi-teacher weighting, layer-wise and task-aware filters, progressive module replacement, and combinations of pruning with distillation.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: The Continuing Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Hybrid Paths Forward
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a flexible, powerful approach for compressing large deep models into faster, smaller students that preserve much of teacher quality. Its success depends on what form of teacher knowledge is transferred (soft outputs, internal representations, attention maps, or decision-boundary signals), on controlling the teacher–student capacity gap, and on task-specific choices. Recent work shows important improvements by (1) selecting or producing student-friendly teachers, (2) distilling internal representations and task-relevant features rather than only logits, (3) using curriculum-like or route-aware teacher schedules, and (4) combining KD with structured pruning or task-aware layer selection. For NLP, practical choices (e.g., shrink-and-fine-tune, pseudo-labeling, layer-wise matching) interact with dataset properties and target abstraction, so hybrid strategies that adapt which knowledge to transfer and when are most effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.
